# The task

In `motif.qmd` we wrote EM for motif finding and tested it on
simulated data, where we knew the answer. Today you work on real
ChIP-seq peaks from ENCODE, where the data are messier, and see how
well several methods recover the known motif of a transcription
factor. Everything here is R, with no external programs to install.

Each group gets one transcription factor:

| TF | Cell line | Function | Canonical motif |
|----|-----------|----------|-----------------|
| cJun | K562 | AP-1 subunit (bZIP); immediate early response to growth signals and stress | TGASTCA |
| cMyc | K562 | basic helix-loop-helix, partner MAX; drives growth and proliferation genes | CACGTG |
| NFYA | K562 | subunit of NF-Y, which binds the CCAAT box near promoters; cell cycle genes | CCAAT |
| YY1 | GM12878 | zinc finger protein; activates or represses, and helps form enhancer-promoter loops | GCCATNTT |
| STAT1 | K562, after interferon gamma | JAK-STAT signal transducer; enters the nucleus on interferon signaling | TTCCNGGAA |
| CEBPB | HepG2, after forskolin | bZIP factor; regulates liver and fat metabolism, inflammation, and differentiation | TTGCGCAA |
| Pol2 | K562 | enzyme that transcribes mRNA; recruited by TFs, not sequence specific | none (promoters sometimes have a TATA box, TATAAA) |

In these motifs S is G or C and N is any nucleotide. A motif is written
5' to 3' on one of the two strands, so what you find may be the
reverse complement of what is written here (more on this below). These
are the motifs reported in the literature and in JASPAR, and your
analysis does not have to agree with them exactly.

For each TF the file `chip_seqs.rds` has the 500 peaks with the
strongest signal. Each peak is 200 bp centered on the summit of the
peak (hg38 sequence). The script `chip_make_data.R` shows how these
were made from the ENCODE peak calls in AnnotationHub.

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(Biostrings)
library(universalmotif)
library(here)
rds_file <- here("model", "chip_seqs.rds")
if (!file.exists(rds_file)) {
  download.file("https://github.com/biodatascience/compbio/raw/refs/heads/gh-pages/model/chip_seqs.rds",
                rds_file, mode="wb")
}
chip_seqs <- readRDS(rds_file)
names(chip_seqs)
tf <- "cJun" # change this to your TF
peaks <- chip_seqs[[tf]]$peaks
peaks
```

# Packages used

You need these installed (all from CRAN or Bioconductor):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
BiocManager::install(c("Biostrings", "universalmotif", "MotifDb", "kernlab", "here"))
```

* *Biostrings*: counting k-mers and matching patterns
* *universalmotif*: motif logos, shuffling sequences, scanning for
  motifs, and comparing a motif you found to a database of known motifs
* *MotifDb*: a database of known motifs (JASPAR, HOCOMOCO and others)
* *kernlab*: support vector machines with a string kernel
* *here*: locating files relative to the root of the course repository

# Both strands

DNA has two strands, and a transcription factor can bind a site on
either one. The motif we write down is the sequence read 5' to 3' on
one strand, and on the other strand the same site reads as the
reverse complement. For example, the AP-1 site `TGAGTCA` reads as
`TGACTCA` on the other strand:

```{r}
reverseComplement(DNAString("TGAGTCA"))
```

The peak sequences in `chip_seqs.rds` are all given on the forward
strand of the genome, so a binding site is equally likely to appear as
the motif or as its reverse complement. Each method below handles this
in a different way:

* k-mer counts (Method 1) with `oligonucleotideFrequency` count the
  forward strand only, so a k-mer and its reverse complement are
  counted separately. We will add the reverse complement of each
  sequence, as EM does, to count both strands.
* EM (Method 2) adds the reverse complement of every peak to the data,
  as extra sequences, so that windows on both strands are tested.
* comparing to JASPAR (Method 2) and scanning for motifs (Method 4) are
  done with `tryRC=TRUE` and `RC=TRUE`, which also test the reverse
  complement of the motif.
* the string kernel SVM (Method 3) is not strand aware, and counts the
  forward strand only. Expect to see a k-mer and its reverse complement
  both near the top of the weights.

Because of this, the motif you find from EM may be the reverse
complement of the motif in the table above, and that is not a
problem. `motif_rc(mot)` in *universalmotif* does the same operation for a motif
object.

# Method 1: counting k-mers (the baseline)

The simplest idea is to count all k-mers in the peaks and ask which are
more common than expected. We need a control set of sequences for "what
we would expect". The choice of control turns out to matter a lot.

First try the sequence 2 kb to the right of each peak as control:

```{r}
kmer_enrich <- function(peaks, control, k) {
  fp <- colSums(oligonucleotideFrequency(peaks, k))
  fc <- colSums(oligonucleotideFrequency(control, k))
  sort((fp + 1) / (fc + 1), decreasing=TRUE)
}
head(kmer_enrich(peaks, chip_seqs[[tf]]$control, k=6))
```

Now a different control: shuffle each peak sequence, preserving its
dinucleotide counts (`k=2`). Any enrichment of longer k-mers is then
not explained by the nucleotide or dinucleotide composition of the
peaks.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
shuffled <- shuffle_sequences(peaks, k=2)
head(kmer_enrich(peaks, shuffled, k=6))
```

Counting the forward strand only splits the signal between a k-mer and
its reverse complement. To count both strands, we add the reverse
complement of each sequence to the set before counting. A k-mer and
its reverse complement then have the same count, so we keep only one
of each pair (the one that comes first alphabetically).

```{r}
kmer_enrich_both <- function(peaks, control, k) {
  count_both <- function(s) {
    colSums(oligonucleotideFrequency(c(s, reverseComplement(s)), k))
  }
  fp <- count_both(peaks)
  fc <- count_both(control)
  enrich <- sort((fp + 1) / (fc + 1), decreasing=TRUE)
  rc <- as.character(reverseComplement(DNAStringSet(names(enrich))))
  enrich[names(enrich) <= rc]
}
head(kmer_enrich_both(peaks, shuffled, k=6))
```

Notes:

* The two controls can give different top k-mers. Compare them for a few
  of the other TFs too. Peaks are often in promoters, which are GC rich
  and have many CpG dinucleotides, and the shifted control is not
  matched for this, while the shuffled control is.
* Try `k` of 5, 6, 7, and 8. As `k` grows, each k-mer is seen fewer
  times, so the counts get smaller and the enrichment values get more
  variable. A k-mer and its reverse complement are the same binding
  site on the opposite strand, and both show up in the forward-strand
  list above.

# Method 2: EM

The file `chip_em.R` has the EM algorithm from `motif.qmd`, adapted to
real data. The changes are:

* it takes a `DNAStringSet`, and uses the central 100 bp of each peak
  (`trim`) because the motif is usually near the summit
* it looks on both strands, by adding the reverse complement of each
  sequence
* it adds a small pseudocount, so that no entry of $\theta$ is exactly 0
* as in MEME, you can start from a k-mer (`seed`) instead of from
  random values

Reading the function, find where each of these happens. You need to
choose the width `w` of the motif. Start around 8 to 10.

```{r}
source(here("model", "chip_em.R"))
set.seed(1)
system.time({
  fit <- em_motif(peaks, w=8, n_starts=10)
})
round(fit$theta, 2)
fit$n_motif # number of windows estimated to be motifs
```

To look at the result, we use the *universalmotif* package, which draws
the logo of a position probability matrix. The height of each letter is
its probability times the information content of the column.

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.5}
mot <- create_motif(fit$theta, alphabet="DNA", name=tf, type="PPM")
mot@alphabet <- "DNA" # so that the labels agree with those in MotifDb
view_motifs(mot)
```

Then we compare this motif to a database of known human motifs. Here
we use JASPAR (2024) through *MotifDb*. The comparison is by Pearson
correlation of the matrices, trying both strands.

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(MotifDb)
is_jaspar_human <- values(MotifDb)$dataSource == "jaspar2024" &
  values(MotifDb)$organism == "Hsapiens"
jaspar <- convert_motifs(MotifDb[is_jaspar_human],
                         class="universalmotif-universalmotif")
match_jaspar <- function(mot, n=5) {
  res <- compare_motifs(c(list(mot), jaspar), compare.to=1,
                        method="PCC", min.overlap=6, tryRC=TRUE)
  as.data.frame(res)[seq_len(n), c("target","score","Eval")]
}
match_jaspar(mot)
```

You can also see how well your motif lines up with a motif from the
database, with `view_motifs(list(mot, jaspar[["name of the motif"]]))`.

Notes:

* The result depends on the starting values and on the width `w`. Rerun
  with a different `set.seed()` or width, and compare the motifs and
  `fit$loglik`. The fit with the highest log likelihood is the one kept
  from the random starts.
* EM can get stuck in repetitive sequence such as poly-A, which has
  little to do with binding sites. Under the simple background model
  (a single set of nucleotide frequencies), poly-A windows are unlikely,
  so a poly-A motif fits the data better than the background does.
  Masking repeats, or a background model that looks at neighboring
  nucleotides, are ways to avoid this.
* If the random starts fail, start EM from your best k-mer from
  Method 1 with `seed="TGACTCA"` (any k-mer up to width `w`). This is
  similar to how MEME picks starting values.
* `fit$n_motif` can be larger than the number of peaks (about 500). The
  model treats overlapping windows as independent, it searches both
  strands, and a motif can read almost the same on both strands. Method
  4 is a better way to say how many peaks contain the motif.

# Method 3: support vector machine with a string kernel

Methods 1 and 2 look for a pattern shared by the peaks. We can also ask
for a classifier which distinguishes peaks from control sequence, and
then look inside the classifier to see which k-mers it uses.

A string kernel measures similarity of two sequences by the number of
sub-strings of length $k$ they have in common (the "spectrum" kernel).
We use *kernlab* as in the `bioc` homework. kernlab expects a list of
character strings.

```{r}
library(kernlab)
set.seed(1)
y <- factor(rep(c("peak", "control"), each=length(peaks)))
s <- as.list(c(as.character(peaks), as.character(shuffled)))
sk <- stringdot(type="spectrum", length=6, normalized=TRUE)
system.time({
  svm_fit <- ksvm(s, y, kernel=sk, C=1, cross=5)
})
svm_fit
# fraction of held-out sequences correctly called peak or control
1 - cross(svm_fit)
```

The cross validation accuracy is the fraction of held-out sequences
(left out of the fit, in 5 folds) that are correctly called as a peak or
as control. Half of the sequences are peaks, so 0.5 is chance. This tells
us how well peaks can be told apart from the shuffled control, using
only 6-mer content. A support vector
machine is a weighted sum over the training sequences, and for the
spectrum kernel that is the same as a weight for every 6-mer. We
compute the weights for each 6-mer, from the sequences chosen as
support vectors:

```{r}
kmer_weights <- function(svm_fit, seqs, k) {
  counts <- oligonucleotideFrequency(DNAStringSet(unlist(seqs)), k)
  counts <- counts / sqrt(rowSums(counts^2)) # the kernel was normalized
  sv <- SVindex(svm_fit)
  w <- drop(coef(svm_fit)[[1]] %*% counts[sv,])
  names(w) <- colnames(counts)
  sort(w, decreasing=TRUE)
}
w <- kmer_weights(svm_fit, s, 6)
head(w)
tail(w)
```

The k-mers with large positive weights push a sequence toward being
called a peak. Compare the top of this list to the top k-mers
from Method 1. The weights are for the forward strand only, so look for
a k-mer and its reverse complement both having large weights.

Notes:

* The SVM can use combinations of k-mers that together distinguish
  peaks from control, and so it is less affected than the enrichment in
  Method 1 by many related k-mers that share the same underlying motif.
* Try other values of `length` (4 to 8) and `C`, and note how the cross
  validation accuracy and the time per fit change.
* Using the shifted control from Method 1 instead of shuffled
  sequences changes what the classifier can learn. Peaks and shifted
  sequences differ in GC content and CpG content in addition to motifs.

# Method 4: scanning for a known motif

Once you have a candidate motif (from EM, or from a database), you can
ask how many peaks contain it, relative to control sequence.
`scan_sequences` slides the motif along each sequence, and reports
windows with a log-odds score above a threshold, on either strand.

```{r}
hits_in <- function(mot, seqs, pvalue=1e-4) {
  res <- scan_sequences(mot, seqs, threshold=pvalue, threshold.type="pvalue",
                        RC=TRUE, verbose=0, nthreads=1)
  length(unique(res$sequence)) / length(seqs)
}
c(peaks=hits_in(mot, peaks), shuffled=hits_in(mot, shuffled))
```

Notes:

* Compare the fraction of peaks with a match to the fraction in the
  control, and to the proportion of peaks you expected to have the motif
  from `fit$n_motif`.
* The fraction depends on the p-value threshold. Try a few values.
* The `chip_seqs` list has the peaks of the other TFs, so you can look
  for your motif in them. For example, look for the cJun motif in the
  cMyc peaks.

# Other tools

These are worth knowing about, but need more time than we have today:

* *monaLisa* and *motifmatchr* (Bioconductor) scan the peaks for all
  JASPAR motifs at once, and test for enrichment. These are fast, and
  they answer the question "which known motifs are over-represented in
  my peaks" rather than finding a new motif.
* The MEME suite (MEME, STREME, FIMO) is the standard tool for de novo
  motif finding, and what EM here is modeled on. It is a separate
  program rather than an R package, and *universalmotif* and *memes*
  can call it if it is installed. We skip it here so that nothing has
  to be installed outside of R.
* *gkmSVM* and neural networks (deep learning models of TF binding)
  extend the idea of Method 3 to gapped k-mers or to learned filters.
* Deep learning models trained on genome-wide data, such as ChromBPNet
  (trained on chromatin accessibility, ATAC-seq or DNase-seq) and
  AlphaGenome (trained on many assays, including ChIP-seq of TFs),
  predict the signal at every base pair of a sequence, and can be used
  to locate motifs by *in silico mutagenesis*. We take a peak region,
  and for each position change the base to each of the other three
  bases, and ask how much the predicted signal in the peak drops.
  (Faster attribution methods such as DeepLIFT approximate this.)
  Positions where mutations strongly reduce the signal are those that matter for
  binding, and a run of adjacent such positions is a motif. Unlike
  Methods 1 to 3, this does not require a control set of sequences, but
  it does require a trained model, and the models are used from Python
  (and typically need a GPU, or a server), so we do not run them here.
